title: Session Persistence
description: Explore session persistence strategies including sticky sessions, session replication, and shared session stores to maintain user context across load-balanced servers.

data.text: Many web applications maintain user state on the server between requests. When requests are distributed across multiple backend servers, the load balancer must ensure that subsequent requests from the same user reach the server holding that users session. This requirement is known as session persistence.

Sticky sessions, also called session affinity, instruct the load balancer to route all requests from a given client to the same backend server. This is often implemented using cookies or source IP hashing. While simple, sticky sessions reduce load balancing effectiveness and can cause uneven distribution during traffic spikes.

data.title: Trade-off
data.text: Sticky sessions simplify implementation but hurt fault tolerance. If the sticky server fails, users lose their session unless failover is handled explicitly.

A more scalable approach stores session data in a shared backend such as Redis or a database. Because any server can retrieve the session, the load balancer is free to route requests freely. This removes the need for sticky sessions and supports rolling deployments and autoscaling without session loss.

Session replication copies session state between application servers. It can be in-memory or database-backed. While replication keeps sessions available during failover, it increases network traffic and memory usage, and it complicates scaling when servers are added or removed frequently.

data.caption: Three common approaches to maintaining session state across backend servers.

terms.definition: Routing all requests from a single client to the same backend server.
A cookie set by the load balancer to enforce session affinity.
A shared backend such as Redis that holds session data accessible to all servers.

data.title: Choosing a strategy
items: Use sticky sessions for small deployments with low churn.
Use a shared session store for cloud-native, horizontally scaled systems.
Avoid session replication in environments with frequent scaling events.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Sticky sessions are easy but limit scalability and resilience.
Shared stores such as Redis allow free request routing.
Choose the strategy that matches your scaling and failure tolerance requirements.
data.takeaway: Stateless services with shared session storage are generally more resilient than sticky-session architectures.
